title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Spinal Cord Injuries – A NAEMSP Comprehensive Review and Analysis of the Literature
condition_or_topic: Prehospital management of traumatic spinal cord injury, with emphasis on spinal immobilization, spinal motion restriction (SMR), and delayed neurological injury.
clinical_background: Prehospital use of backboards and cervical collars became standard practice largely because movement after spinal injury was thought to cause later neurological deterioration. SMR was subsequently introduced as an approach intended to limit movement without necessarily using a backboard. Both practices rest on an uncertain clinical benefit, while immobilization devices have documented potential to cause harm. The review examines whether the proposed mechanism of delayed injury and the continued use of these practices are supported by the literature.
objectives: Assess the proposed causes of delayed neurological injury after trauma, focusing on spinal movement, hypoxia, and hypoperfusion.
Examine patient harms associated with backboards and cervical collars, particularly pressure ulcers, respiratory impairment, increased intracranial pressure, and direct neurological harm.
Evaluate whether backboards and cervical collars prevent delayed neurological injury or restrict spinal movement as intended.
Assess whether patient anxiety, anatomy, age, or environmental conditions affect the utility of backboards and cervical collars.
clinical_question: In patients with trauma and possible spinal cord injury (P), does prehospital spinal immobilization using a backboard and cervical collar, or SMR using a cervical collar (I), compared with care without those devices or with alternative movement-restriction approaches (C), prevent delayed neurological injury or limit spinal movement, and what patient harms are associated with their use (O)?
study_design: Structured literature review within the NAEMSP Trauma Compendium Series. A librarian-assisted strategy searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science on April 19, 2023, with updated searches on June 1, 2024 and February 1, 2025. The authors also searched references and reviewer-suggested manuscripts. One reviewer screened titles and abstracts; two reviewers assessed full manuscripts, with the first author resolving disagreements and reviewing manuscripts selected for full analysis. Data were extracted using a standardized form in Covidence and organized around four research questions.

population.description: Published human and animal studies containing patient data relevant to delayed neurological injury after trauma or to spinal immobilization and spinal motion restriction. No single patient cohort was enrolled for this review.
inclusion_criteria: Human or animal studies that addressed at least one of the four research questions and included patient data.
exclusion_criteria: Abstracts without full publication in a peer-reviewed journal.
Editorial letters, other reviews or meta-analyses, clinical practice guidelines, and book chapters.
Full manuscripts published in languages other than English.
population.care_setting: Primarily prehospital trauma care; the eligible literature also included studies conducted during hospital care.

interventions: Spinal immobilization using a backboard and cervical collar. For this review, a backboard encompassed devices intended to immobilize the entire spinal column, including rigid spine boards, Kendrick extrication device (KED), boards with head blocks, strapping materials, and vacuum splints.
Cervical-collar immobilization alone, using either hard or soft collars.
comparators: Care without spinal immobilization or without a cervical collar, where evaluated in the included studies.
Comparisons among immobilization devices or approaches, where evaluated in the included studies.

primary: Potential causes of delayed neurological injury after trauma, particularly movement, hypoxia, and hypoperfusion.
Patient harms associated with backboards or cervical collars, particularly pressure ulcers, respiratory depression, increased intracranial pressure, and direct nervous-system injury.
Effectiveness of backboards and cervical collars in preventing delayed neurological injury or limiting spinal-column movement.
Effects of patient anxiety, anatomy, age, and environmental conditions on the utility of backboards and cervical collars.

interpretation: The authors conclude that spinal immobilization and spinal motion restriction cause substantial harm, sometimes potentially life-threatening, while published evidence does not establish a definitive clinical benefit. Evidence linking movement after injury to delayed neurological deterioration is also inconclusive. If delayed deterioration occurs, its causes are likely multifactorial; the reviewed evidence more strongly supports a possible role for spinal cord hypoperfusion than for movement, without proving causation. Devices intended to restrict motion may fail to do so and can sometimes increase unintended spinal movement.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Historical practice and subsequent guidance treated movement after spinal injury as a cause of paralysis, although the supporting reports by Rogers, Geisler, and Toscano relied on anecdotal observations rather than stronger evidence. The authors note that reports favoring movement as the explanation preceded widespread MRI use, whereas the studies implicating hypoperfusion and other vascular insults followed it. Their findings also challenge the historical assumption that immobilization is safer than withholding it.
clinical_implications: Concentrating on motion restriction could divert clinicians' attention from shock and hypoperfusion.
Pressure-related impairment of tissue blood supply can begin when a device is applied, rather than only after prolonged use.
The possibility that movement contributes to delayed neurological deterioration cannot be excluded, despite the absence of definitive evidence establishing that mechanism.
Potential device-related harms and the uncertain benefit make patient comfort, informed consent and patient autonomy relevant to care.
practice_implications: EMS clinicians should prioritize resuscitation and the management of shock and hypoperfusion while maintaining patient comfort.
The authors consider coaching and shared decision-making reasonable ways to minimize gross spinal movement where possible without immobilization devices.
Efforts to reduce cervical collar use should be considered; backboards and full body vacuum splints should be limited to active patient extrication.
Spinal immobilization and spinal motion restriction should no longer be upheld as standard care in light of the documented harms and the lack of evidence establishing clinical benefit.

Emergency medical services physicians should lead clinician education and quality-management programs concerning recognition of possible spinal cord injury and application of these findings. EMS leaders should work with local trauma-system leaders on changes in practice and a renewed emphasis on resuscitation.
EMS protocols for suspected spinal cord injury should use techniques with demonstrated benefit.
EMS systems should account for physiological differences when selecting a MAP threshold for pediatric trauma patients.
For traumatic shock, EMS systems should consider a range of treatment approaches and may need to mobilize advanced life support resources not otherwise used for these patients.
limitations: Most included studies were retrospective and subject to bias and uncontrolled confounding.

The evidence favoring hypoperfusion over movement consists of associations from retrospective case-control and cohort studies; it cannot establish causation. Hypotension could result from spinal cord injury rather than cause its worsening.
Because the review did not distinguish hard from soft collars, it cannot determine whether soft collars are safer.
The studies addressing hypoperfusion involved adults. The authors found no pediatric target MAPs linked to neurological outcomes.
The evidence on perfusion derives primarily from inpatient care, and prospective studies of optimal MAPs in the EMS setting are unavailable.

The review cannot determine the best way to manage hypoperfusion in patients with possible spinal cord injury. Its focus on delayed neurological deterioration does not encompass every consequence of multisystem trauma.
strengths: The authors used a broad search strategy and allowed additional studies to be identified through hand searches.
open_questions: Whether delayed neurological injury develops after trauma as a distinct phenomenon, rather than representing an injury present at impact that evolves over time.
Whether movement after injury contributes to delayed neurological deterioration and, if it does, how its role compares with hypoperfusion.
Whether hypotension contributes to worsening spinal cord injury or is instead a consequence of the injury.
Whether soft collars offer benefit without increasing pressure ulcers, impairing vascular flow or causing other harms.
What MAP thresholds correspond to neurological outcomes in pediatric patients and what MAPs are optimal in the EMS setting.
Which approach best manages hypoperfusion in patients with possible spinal cord injury.
future_directions: Investigate whether soft collars provide benefit without the harms identified by the authors.
Conduct prospective studies specific to the EMS setting to examine optimal MAPs.
Pursue further research on EMS care for patients with possible spinal cord injury.
NAEMSP should review and update the document every five years after publication, including a search and synthesis of newly published relevant evidence.

main_findings.description: The review found documented harms from immobilization but no definitive clinical benefit from spinal immobilization or spinal motion restriction (SMR).
main_findings.context: The count refers to studies documenting harms. The authors found no studies demonstrating a definitive benefit from spinal immobilization.

main_findings.description: Evidence linking delayed neurological injury to spinal cord hypoperfusion was stronger than evidence implicating post-injury movement, although the reported associations do not establish causation.
main_findings.context: The studies associated neurological outcomes with perfusion; three retrospective cohort studies related outcomes directly to reported mean arterial pressures (MAP).

main_findings.description: The review identified studies associating post-injury movement with delayed neurological deficits, but both were case series with potential confounding, including hypoperfusion.
main_findings.context: The authors found no additional manuscripts identifying post-injury movement as a pathophysiological cause.

main_findings.description: Clark et al. associated higher prehospital MAP with greater odds of neurological improvement after spinal cord injury.
main_findings.metric: average increase in odds per increase in prehospital MAP
main_findings.context: The study included 99 patients and reported an inflection point MAP of 85 mmHg.

main_findings.description: Haldrup et al. associated fewer prehospital hypotensive episodes with better neurological recovery at one year.
main_findings.context: Hypotension was defined as MAP < 80 mmHg; the study assessed episodes during prehospital care, in the operating room, and in the neuro-intensive care unit.

main_findings.description: In the entire cohort analyzed by Chen et al., immobilization was not associated with improved neurological outcomes in multivariable logistic regression.
main_findings.context: This was the overall-cohort analysis, rather than the cervical cord injury subgroup analysis.

main_findings.description: Hauswald et al. reported less neurological disability among patients who had not been immobilized than among those who had been immobilized.
main_findings.context: In this retrospective comparison, 120 patients at the University of Malaya received no spinal immobilization, whereas 334 patients at the University of New Mexico received spinal immobilization. The review notes differences between the systems and lack of adjustment for non-spinal injury severity.

main_findings.description: Beyond the Chen et al. subgroup result, the review found no manuscripts clearly showing that immobilization prevents delayed neurological injury; other manuscripts reported unchanged deficits or worsening injury after device application.
main_findings.context: The authors describe the clinical significance of the Chen et al. finding as questionable.

main_findings.description: Studies of spinal movement produced conflicting findings: immobilization limited movement in some studies, made no measurable difference in others, and increased movement after device application in others.
main_findings.context: Meusch and Rahmatalla described exaggerated movement at the neck–sternum junction during fore-aft vehicle vibration.

main_findings.description: Studies of protocols that omitted cervical collars or eliminated backboards did not report an increase in delayed neurological injury.
main_findings.context: The cervical-collar studies included patients subsequently found to have cervical spine injuries who had been transported without cervical immobilization.

notable_adverse_events: Immobilization devices increased tissue pressure and reduced tissue perfusion, creating a risk of pressure ulcers; these effects could begin within minutes of application. The review also identified pressure-related findings with cervical collars alone and tissue pressures with vacuum splints similar to those of padded long spine boards.
In a cited study of anesthetized patients, cervical collars caused complete airway obstruction in five patients.

Cited studies reported respiratory compromise with immobilization, including statistically significant reductions in forced vital capacity and forced expiratory volume in one second among healthy volunteers. A vacuum splint did not avert statistically significant reductions in pulmonary function indices.

Cited studies measured increased intracranial pressure after cervical collar application. A cited case report described neurological improvement after collar removal in a patient with cerebral edema on CT.
Jung et al. reported worse neurological outcomes with cervical spine immobilization in patients with traumatic brain injury when MAP was decreased.
Ben-Galim et al. reported significant separation after cervical collar application in nine cadavers with a surgically created C2 fracture, ranging from 3.23–9.23 millimeters.
Immobilization devices could conceal injuries. Hussain and Corsar described a scalp injury missed beneath a cervical collar that required operative washout and repair.
Klein et al. reported potentially life-threatening non-skeletal neck injuries missed in 151 out of 2,267 (6.7%) patients with blast injuries; 0.83% of that cohort had cervical spine injuries.

The review identified delays in care associated with immobilization devices. Haut et al. reported a two-fold increase in mortality among patients with penetrating trauma placed on a backboard and attributed it to treatment delays.

Immobilization was associated with pain and discomfort and with increased use of diagnostic radiology. Leonard et al. reported cervical radiography in 56.6% vs. 13.4% of immobilized versus non-immobilized pediatric patients, respectively (OR 8.2, 95% CI 4.5 − 15.4).

In contrast to reports of greater radiology use, Ward et al. found no change in diagnostic radiology use after a pediatric protocol changed from compulsory backboards and collars to modified SMR: 20% vs 18%, OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.66 − 1.07. The revised protocol still required cervical collars for all trauma patients and backboards for pediatric patients unable to walk independently.

Studies reported that cervical collars distorted pediatric anatomy. Geriatric patients spent longer in immobilization devices than a younger cohort and were at risk of dysphagia and respiratory failure.

subgroup_analyses: In Chen et al.'s subgroup with cervical cord injury, spinal immobilization was associated with a statistically significant favorable outcome (aOR 3.14, 95% CI 1.04 − 9.50, p = 0.043). The review cautions that the study defined a favorable outcome as modified Rankin score (mRS) 0–3, which could include moderate disability at mRS 3; the subgroup analysis did not control for blood pressure and excluded patients with traumatic brain injury.
Within the Chen et al. cervical cord injury subgroup, the reported favorable association was most pronounced among patients with ISS > 9 (aOR 5.50, 95% CI 1.02 − 29.69, p = 0.048).

In Chen et al.'s overall database of 759 patients, those with ISS > 9 had worse neurological outcomes with spinal immobilization (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.17 − 0.72, p = 0.004). This is a separate analysis from the favorable finding in the cervical cord injury subgroup with ISS > 9.

In Chen et al.'s overall database, patients who received prehospital fluid management had worse neurological outcomes with spinal immobilization (aOR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19 − 0.84, p = 0.016). Prehospital fluid management was reported in 4.4% of patients with a favorable outcome versus 19.8% with an unfavorable outcome; the review raises possible confounding by hypoperfusion.
The review found no literature clearly establishing that anxiety or environmental conditions changed the utility of immobilization devices.
secondary_results: After duplicates were removed, reviewers screened 3944 manuscripts: 3500 from the search performed in 2023, 300 from 2024, and 144 from 2025. They reviewed 769 full manuscripts and selected 99 for full analysis: 93 from the initial search, 2 from the 2024 search, and 4 from the 2025 search. Hand searching considered another 18 studies and added 16, yielding 115 manuscripts in the review.

Because some manuscripts addressed more than one question, 14 studies concerned the pathophysiology of delayed neurological injury, 55 concerned harms, 58 concerned immobilization effectiveness, and 7 concerned other factors.

Geisler et al. stated that they examined 29 patients with delayed symptoms but provided individual data for only two. One developed permanent paralysis at T4 after a car crash in 1955 and also had hypoperfusion, a depressed skull fracture, and thoracic tenderness; another developed leg weakness on standing after a car crash in 1949 and improved with physical therapy. The review identifies insufficient clinical detail and possible confounding in attributing either course to handling.

Toscano's retrospective case series described 9 patients whose neurological deficits began during ambulance care. The cited author could not determine whether deterioration reflected post-injury movement or another pathophysiological process.

A questionnaire-based study of 68 patients with cervical cord injury reported better outcomes after transport while lying down than after transport while sitting; the review states that either movement or relative spinal cord hypoperfusion could explain the finding.

The review also identified cord edema or contusions, epidural hematomas, and vascular injury as potential contributors to delayed neurological deficits; these processes might also involve reduced perfusion.
The reviewed studies did not establish whether soft collars are safer than hard collars. The authors note reports of pressure ulcers with soft collars and similar rates of neurological deficits.

The studies linking hypoperfusion to neurological outcomes involved adults; the review found no pediatric target MAP linked to neurological outcomes and no prospective study of optimal MAP in the EMS setting.

main_conclusion: The authors find no published evidence establishing a clinical benefit from spinal immobilization or spinal motion restriction sufficient to maintain either as standard care, whereas harms are documented. narrative_summary:
This structured review examined proposed causes of delayed neurological injury after trauma, harms of immobilization, and whether backboards and cervical collars prevent injury or adequately restrict spinal movement. Searches of PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science, supplemented by reference searches and later search updates, yielded 115 manuscripts from 3944 screened. Because some studies addressed several questions, 14 concerned pathophysiology, 55 examined harms, 58 evaluated effectiveness, and 7 addressed other factors.

The authors found stronger evidence associating spinal cord hypoperfusion with worse neurological outcomes than evidence attributing delayed deficits to post-injury movement. The movement hypothesis rested on two case series; an association with hypoperfusion does not, however, establish causation. Studies documented pressure injury, respiratory effects, increased intracranial pressure, missed injuries, delays and pain. Findings on movement restriction varied, and no definitive clinical benefit from immobilization was established. One study reported a favorable cervical-cord-injury subgroup result, but not an improvement across its full cohort.

For prehospital practice, the authors favor attention to resuscitation, shock, hypoperfusion and patient comfort rather than routine immobilization. They propose considering less cervical-collar use and limiting backboards and full-body vacuum splints to active extrication. Most included studies were retrospective, and the review could not establish an optimal prehospital perfusion target or the best way to treat hypoperfusion.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Spinal immobilization uses a backboard and cervical collar, whereas spinal motion restriction (SMR) requires a cervical collar and can use a vacuum splint or ambulance cot. Both became established prehospital trauma practices on the premise that movement after injury could produce delayed neurological deficits, despite possible harms and no definitive evidence of clinical benefit. This review assessed proposed causes of delayed neurological injury and the benefits and harms of both practices. The authors conducted a structured review for the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP) Trauma Compendium Series, searching PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science for relevant literature dating back to 1900. Of 3944 manuscripts screened, 115 were identified. Because some addressed more than one question, 14 examined the pathophysiology of delayed neurological injury, 55 examined harms, 58 examined effectiveness, and 7 examined other factors. Two case series proposed movement after injury as a cause of delayed neurological injury. Eight retrospective studies, including two case control studies and three retrospective cohort studies, associated hypoperfusion with neurological worsening. The review identified 55 studies reporting harms and none establishing a definitive benefit from spinal immobilization. The authors conclude that published evidence does not support spinal immobilization or SMR as standard care. They advise considering efforts to reduce cervical collar use and limiting backboards and full body vacuum splints to active extrication.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Concern about movement in patients with possible spinal cord injury arose during the Second World War. Howlett proposed that excessive movement with vertebral fractures could produce neck or back hyperflexion or hyperextension and irreversible cord damage; transport in an anatomically aligned, padded position was recommended. In the 1950s and 1960s, two case series proposing that movement after injury could cause paralysis and three instructional papers on transferring patients from cars onto hard boards helped establish immobilization. In 1957, Rogers reviewed 87 patients treated for cervical spine injury, of whom eight reported delayed neurological deficits. Rogers attributed paralysis to cervical movement before definitive treatment and proposed that a collar of his own design could have prevented it. Despite evidence limited to uncontrolled case reports and retrospective causal claims, the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons (AAOS) presented immobilization as standard care in a 1971 emergency medical services (EMS) textbook. Its guidance called for splinting and long-backboard transport without excessive spinal movement and warned that movement with a broken neck might contribute to paralysis or death. This approach paralleled splinting of other bone injuries; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) did not become available to characterize cord injury until the late 1980s. Evidence of pain, respiratory suppression, and pressure ulcers from hard boards prompted NAEMSP and the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT) to advise judicious backboard use in 2013, accompanied by a 2014 resource document, because harms might outweigh the presumed, unproven benefit. Updated 2018 guidance from ACS-COT, the American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and NAEMSP treated immobilization and SMR as the same underlying concept. It distinguished backboards for immobilization from devices such as scoop stretchers, vacuum splints, and ambulance cots for SMR, while continuing to advocate cervical collars to limit neck movement. A 2013 guideline from the American Association of Neurological Surgeons and the Congress of Neurological Surgeons likewise presented rigid collars as limiting cervical movement and thereby preventing delayed injury, relying on a case series. From proposals in the 1940s to adoption as standard care in the 1970s, movement of an unstable spine was repeatedly treated as the cause of delayed deficits. The authors identify scant literature establishing either that causal claim or a clinical benefit from immobilization or SMR. Their aim was to assess the pathophysiology of delayed neurological injury after trauma, the effectiveness of movement-restricting practices, and their documented harms relative to possible benefit.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: For the NAEMSP Trauma Compendium Series, the authors and a trained medical librarian developed one search strategy addressing four questions: whether movement, hypoxia, or hypoperfusion causes delayed neurological injury after trauma; whether backboards or cervical collars cause pressure ulcers, respiratory depression, increased intracranial pressure, or direct nervous-system harm; whether these devices prevent delayed injury or limit spinal movement; and whether anxiety, anatomy, age, or environmental conditions affect their utility. The strategy was adapted to the compendium approach and to four databases. Searches were run on April 19, 2023 in PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science using Covidence. The project defined a backboard by its purpose of immobilizing the whole spine, encompassing rigid boards, Kendrick extrication device (KED), boards with head blocks, strapping materials, and vacuum splints. A cervical collar meant any hard or soft collar intended to prevent neck movement, regardless of type or manufacturer. Reviewers considered combined backboard-and-collar immobilization and collar use alone. Eligible publications were peer-reviewed human or animal studies dating back to 1900, available in English, containing patient data, and addressing at least one review question. The authors excluded manikin simulations without human subjects, abstracts without full peer-reviewed publication, editorial letters, other reviews or meta-analysis, clinical practice guidelines, book chapters, and full manuscripts published in other languages from the final analysis; excluded categories could still inform reference searches or the introduction. One reviewer screened titles and abstracts. Two reviewers assessed full manuscripts, with the first author resolving disagreements and independently reviewing every manuscript selected for full analysis. Reviewers used a standardized Covidence form to summarize each study and draw a conclusion relevant to the questions. Exported data were arranged in a master spreadsheet and four question-specific spreadsheets. The first and second authors checked and standardized those spreadsheets, which all reviewers then assessed independently. Additional studies identified through guideline references and reviewers’ suggestions underwent consensus review by the first and second authors. Searches were repeated on June 1, 2024 and February 1, 2025; the first and second authors screened, reviewed, and extracted the additional publications using the same general approach.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: After deduplication, 3944 manuscripts were screened: 3500 from the 2023 search, 300 from 2024, and 144 from 2025. Title and abstract screening led to review of 769 full manuscripts. Database searching yielded 99 manuscripts for full analysis: 93 from the initial search, 2 from 2024, and 4 from 2025. Hand searching identified 18 additional candidates, of which 16 were included, producing a total of 115 manuscripts. Because manuscripts could answer multiple questions, 14 addressed causes of delayed neurological injury, 55 addressed harms of immobilization, 58 addressed effectiveness, and 7 addressed other factors. Table 1 groups proposed causes of delayed injury in relation to the introduction of MRI. Table 2 groups reported harms by publication period relative to the 2013 NAEMSP/ACS-COT and 2018 ACS-COT/ACEP/NAEMSP position statements. Tables 3 and 4 summarize evidence on whether immobilization or SMR limits movement and prevents injury, respectively. Supplemental tables 2–5 are described as providing study-by-study summaries organized by question.

document_sections.heading: Review of the Literature Addressing Research Questions
document_sections.content: The authors present the included literature under the four prespecified questions: possible causes of delayed neurological injury, patient harms from immobilization devices, effectiveness in limiting movement or injury, and factors that could modify device utility.

document_sections.heading: What Are the Underlying Pathophysiological Causes to the Phenomenon of Delayed Neurological Injury in the Setting of Trauma with a Focus on Movement, Hypoxia, and Hypoperfusion?
document_sections.content: The authors judge the evidence supporting spinal cord hypoperfusion as a proposed cause of delayed neurological injury stronger than that supporting movement after injury as the leading cause. Two included case series linked movement with delayed deficits, but both had confounding factors, including possible hypoperfusion. In a 1966 retrospective case series, Geisler et al. used hospital nursing notes to examine changing neurological findings. Although they described 29 patients with delayed symptoms, they presented data for only two. One patient, after a 1955 car crash, had hypoperfusion, a depressed skull fracture, thoracic tenderness, and permanent paralysis at T4. Another, after a 1949 car crash, developed leg weakness on standing that improved with physical therapy. Despite limited injury details, vital signs, and motor examinations, those investigators attributed deterioration to inadequate recognition of instability and handling. In another pre-MRI retrospective case series, Toscano described 9 patients whose deficits reportedly arose during ambulance care. That conclusion relied on interviews without a comparison group; Toscano also acknowledged that movement could not readily be distinguished from other causes of deterioration. Eight studies associated neurological outcomes with perfusion, including three retrospective cohort studies relating outcomes to mean arterial pressure (MAP). In 99 patients with spinal cord injury, Clark et al. reported that each 10 mmHg increase in prehospital MAP corresponded to an average 79% increase in the odds of neurological improvement and identified an inflection point of 85 mmHg. Haldrup et al. defined hypotensive events as MAP < 80 mmHg across prehospital, operating-room, and neuro-intensive-care phases; fewer prehospital events were associated with better neurological recovery at one year (p < 0.001). A questionnaire study of 68 patients with cervical cord injury in Nigeria reported better outcomes after transport lying down than after seated transport, but either movement or relative cord hypoperfusion could explain the difference. The review also identified cord edema or contusions, epidural hematomas, and vascular injury as possible contributors, potentially related to impaired perfusion. Beyond the two case series, it found no manuscripts identifying movement after injury as a pathophysiological cause. Table 1 summarizes the proposed processes and the cited literature by MRI era.

document_sections.heading: Does the Use of a Backboard or Cervical Collar Result in Patient-Oriented Harms with a Focus on the Formation of Decubitus Ulcers, Developing Respiratory Depression, Causing Increased Intra-Cranial Pressure, or Direct Harm to the Nervous System?
document_sections.content: Much of the harm literature concerns pressure ulcers: studies report increased tissue pressure and reduced tissue perfusion with immobilization, including collar use alone. Although vacuum splints may be more comfortable, one study found tissue pressures comparable to those of a padded long spine board. Reduced perfusion and increased ulcer risk can begin within minutes of device application, rather than only after prolonged use. Respiratory studies describe compromise: collars completely obstructed the airway in five anesthetized patients in one study; another found statistically significant reductions in forced vital capacity and forced expiratory volume in one second in healthy volunteers, potentially harmful for patients with respiratory injury. A vacuum splint was more comfortable but did not prevent statistically significant reductions in pulmonary function indices. Studies directly measuring intracranial pressure (ICP) in intensive-care patients report increases after collar application, with impaired venous or cerebral spinal fluid drainage proposed as a mechanism. A case report described neurological improvement after collar removal in a patient with cerebral edema on CT following hanging. In patients with traumatic brain injury and decreased MAP, Jung et al. associated cervical immobilization with worse neurological outcomes. In nine cadavers with surgically created C2 fractures, Ben-Galim et al. observed significant separation of 3.23–9.23 millimeters when a collar was applied. Devices may also obscure injuries or delay care. Hussain and Corsar reported a missed scalp injury requiring operative washout and repair after collar placement. In a blast-injury cohort, Klein et al. reported potentially life threatening non-skeletal neck injuries missed in 151 out of 2,267 (6.7%) patients, including tracheal lacerations and carotid artery dissection; 0.83% of that cohort had cervical spine injuries. The authors interpret immobilization in that setting as exposing patients to missed neck injuries without clinical benefit. Haut et al. reported a two-fold mortality increase among patients with penetrating trauma placed on backboards, which those investigators attributed to treatment delays. Immobilization is also documented to cause pain and discomfort and to increase diagnostic imaging in several studies. Leonard et al. reported more cervical radiography among immobilized than nonimmobilized pediatric patients (56.6% vs. 13.4%, OR 8.2, 95% CI 4.5 − 15.4). Ward et al. reported no change in imaging after a pediatric protocol moved from compulsory backboards and collars to modified SMR (20% vs 18%, OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.66 − 1.07). The authors caution that the statewide protocol still required collars for all trauma patients and full backboard immobilization for pediatric patients unable to walk independently. Table 2 organizes the reported harms by publication period.

document_sections.heading: Are Backboards and Cervical Collars Effective at Preventing Delayed Neurological Injury or Effective at Immobilizing the Spinal Column as Intended?
document_sections.content: The authors identified one study suggesting possible benefit. Using Pan-Asian trauma outcome study data, Chen et al. reported a favorable outcome in a cervical cord injury subgroup associated with immobilization (aOR 3.14, 95% CI 1.04 − 9.50, p = 0.043), particularly for patients with ISS > 9 (aOR 5.50, 95% CI 1.02 − 29.69, p = 0.048). Their adjusted analysis of the full cohort found no neurological improvement (aOR 1.06, 95% CI 0.62 − 1.81, p = 0.826). The review authors identify important methodological problems: Chen et al. defined favorable outcome as modified Rankin score (mRS) 0–3, allowing moderate disability at mRS 3; the cervical subgroup analysis did not adjust for blood pressure and excluded traumatic brain injury. In the overall database of 759 patients, immobilized patients with ISS > 9 and those given prehospital fluids had worse neurological outcomes (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.17 − 0.72, p = 0.004; and aOR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19 − 0.84, p = 0.016, respectively). Prehospital fluids were given to 4.4% of patients with favorable outcomes versus 19.8% with unfavorable outcomes; possible differences in hypoperfusion therefore confound interpretation. Aside from that study’s clinically questionable finding, the review found no manuscript clearly establishing that immobilization prevents delayed neurological injury. Other manuscripts reported unchanged neurological deficits or worsening after device application. In a five-year retrospective comparison published in 1998, Hauswald et al. examined 120 patients without immobilization at the University of Malaya and 334 immobilized patients at the University of New Mexico. They reported less neurological disability among nonimmobilized patients (OR 2.03; 95% CI 1.03 − 3.99; p = 0.04). Differences between the EMS systems and lack of adjustment for non-spinal injury severity limit that comparison, although the authors consider it a challenge to movement as the sole proposed cause. Some included studies found that immobilization reduced measured spinal movement; others found no change or paradoxically increased movement. Meusch and Rahmatalla described exaggerated movement at the neck–sternum junction associated with fore-aft vehicle vibration. Studies in which immobilization was withheld did not report resulting neurological deficits. Studies of field clearance and collar protocol changes reported no increase in delayed injury without collars, including among patients later found to have cervical spine injury. Studies of SMR protocols eliminating backboards also found no increase in delayed injury. Tables 3 and 4 summarize findings on movement and delayed neurological injury.

document_sections.heading: Are There Other Factors That May Affect the Utility of Backboards and Cervical Collars Such as Patient Anxiety, Patient Anatomy, Patient Age, or Environmental Conditions?
document_sections.content: Studies reported that cervical collars can distort pediatric anatomy. Compared with a younger cohort, geriatric patients spent longer in immobilization devices and were at risk of dysphagia and respiratory failure. The review did not find literature clearly demonstrating that anxiety or environmental conditions affect device utility.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The findings challenge the historical assumption that immobilization is safer than foregoing it. The authors deliberately searched broadly and supplemented database searching by hand to investigate whether evidence supports that assumption. They judge the evidence of significant, potentially life-threatening immobilization harms to be compelling and growing, while finding no definitive evidence of clinical benefit from immobilization or other movement-restricting procedures. They also found no definitive evidence that movement after injury produces delayed neurological injury: historical causal claims by Rogers, Geisler, and Toscano rested on anecdotal case observations, although later professional guidance repeated them. The authors question whether injury truly begins after the traumatic event or instead exists at impact and evolves according to its initial severity regardless of subsequent care. If delayed neurological deficits do arise, they consider the evidence for spinal cord hypoperfusion as their primary cause stronger than that for movement, while acknowledging that the pathophysiology may remain uncertain. Manuscripts implicating hypoperfusion and other vascular insults appeared after MRI became available, whereas those proposing movement predated its common use. Even a 1944 proposal to carry patients on boards stressed treating shock. The authors warn that concentrating on motion restriction could distract field clinicians from addressing hypoperfusion. They add that restriction does not consistently limit movement and can increase unintended movement at the cervical–thoracic junction; patients able to respond to pain may also move to relieve discomfort. Because a contribution from movement cannot be ruled out, the authors consider coaching and shared decision making reasonable ways to minimize gross spinal movement without immobilization devices. They reject the premise that positioning intended to restrict movement can avoid skin breakdown: increased tissue pressure restricts blood supply, and that process begins immediately. They frame their interpretation around beneficence, nonmaleficence, patient autonomy, informed consent, and safe, effective, patient-centered care. In their view, the precautionary rationale for immobilization no longer applies; resuscitation and patient comfort should receive greater emphasis. They call for EMS physicians to lead training and quality programs so clinicians can recognize possible spinal cord injury and apply the findings, and for EMS leaders to coordinate changes with local trauma systems. They state that protective protocols should use techniques with demonstrated benefit through an evidence-based approach and call for further research into EMS care for possible spinal cord injury.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: Most included manuscripts were retrospective and susceptible to bias and uncontrolled confounding. The authors’ preference for hypoperfusion over movement as an explanation rests on associations from retrospective case control and cohort studies, not proof of causation; hypotension might result from cord injury rather than cause its worsening. They contrast this uncertainty with the reliance of movement-restriction practice on associations from a small number of case reports. Because the review did not distinguish hard from soft collars, it cannot determine whether soft collars are safer. Soft collars nevertheless appear capable of causing pressure ulcers, while studies reported similar rates of neurological deficits; research is needed to establish whether they offer benefit without more ulcers, impaired vascular flow, or other harm. Hypoperfusion studies involved adults. The review found no pediatric target MAP linked to neurological outcomes; relevant evidence came mainly from inpatient care, with no prospective study of optimal MAP in the EMS setting. EMS systems should account for physiological differences when choosing a pediatric trauma MAP threshold, and prospective EMS studies should be conducted. The review cannot establish the best way to treat hypoperfusion in possible cord injury. Other Trauma Compendium Series papers may address permissive hypotension, crystalloids, blood products, or vasopressors. Its focus was prevention of delayed neurological deficits, whereas trauma can involve multiple organ systems. Because managing traumatic shock likely carries more benefit than harm, EMS systems should consider a range of treatment options and may need advanced life support resources not otherwise deployed for these patients.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: The authors find no literature demonstrating clinical benefit from spinal motion restriction despite its historical acceptance. Attempts to restrict movement cause harms and may paradoxically increase movement. If delayed neurological deficits after trauma exist, their causes are probably multifactorial. EMS clinicians should prioritize shock and hypoperfusion management. The authors advise considering efforts to reduce cervical collar use and restricting backboards and full body vacuum splints to active extrication. Given the absence of evidence for clinical benefit and the evidence of harm, they conclude that spinal immobilization and SMR should no longer be upheld as standard care.
